planting.note: Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this is a non-vining species with no tendrils, so give it open ground rather than a support.

directions: Curlyheads is an uncommon mid-Atlantic and southeastern coastal plain native that forms a low, upright, non-climbing clump covered in silvery-woolly hairs rather than sprawling or twining like most of its relatives. In spring it produces nodding, thick-petaled, pale yellow to cream urn-shaped flowers, followed by the tightly curled, silky seed plumes that give the plant its common name and add interest into summer. It thrives in the same lean, sandy, well-drained soils as many pine-barren and dry-woodland wildflowers, and is best used at the front of a native wildflower bed or rock garden rather than trained on a trellis. Established plants are drought-tolerant and need little care beyond cutting back dead growth in late winter.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in partial shade with roots kept cool, letting the slender stems scramble over rock or through an open shrub.

directions: Rock clematis is the North American counterpart to the Eurasian alpine clematis, found scrambling over rocky slopes, talus, and open montane woodland from the Pacific Northwest through the Rockies. In spring it opens nodding, bell-shaped, violet-blue flowers with slender, pointed petal-like sepals on wiry stems well before most other vines leaf out, followed by fluffy plumed seed heads. It is naturally adapted to thin, rocky, fast-draining soils and cool roots, making it a good fit for a rock garden wall, scree slope, or low fence rather than a large arbor. Prune lightly after flowering since it blooms on the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant in rocky, well-drained, calcareous soil in partial sun; this is a sprawling, essentially non-climbing species best suited to a rock garden or dry slope rather than a trellis.

directions: Addison's leatherflower is a critically imperiled Virginia endemic known only from a handful of dolomite and limestone outcrops in the Ridge and Valley region, where it grows as a low, sprawling, barely climbing perennial rather than a true vine. Its thick, leathery, deep rose-purple to maroon urn-shaped flowers nod from wiry stems in late spring, a close relative in form to the more widespread leatherflowers of the eastern US. Because it is adapted to thin, rocky, well-drained, calcium-rich soils in open woodland, it is a specialist choice for a native rock garden rather than general border use. Its narrow natural range makes it a conservation-interest species for native plant collections.
sources: Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation

planting.note: Plant in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a slope or bank; this low, shrubby species does not need a tall support.

directions: Millboro leatherflower is a critically imperiled, state-listed threatened species found only on a small number of dry shale barrens in western Virginia, where exposed, eroding slate slopes create an open, droughty habitat unlike almost anywhere else in the clematis genus's eastern range. It grows as a low, woody-based, shrubby perennial rather than a climbing vine, producing small, thick-textured, dull purple urn-shaped flowers on short stalks in late spring. Its extreme drought tolerance and preference for lean, shaley, fast-draining ground make it suitable only for a dry rock garden or barren-mimicking bed, not average garden soil. Because of its rarity, it is grown mainly in conservation and native plant society collections.
sources: Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, calcareous soil in partial shade near a fence or shrub to climb; this species prefers the limestone-influenced soils of its native cedar glades.

directions: Morefield's leatherflower is a federally endangered vine known only from a cluster of limestone cedar glades and talus slopes around Huntsville, Alabama, making it one of the rarest species in the entire genus. It climbs weakly through surrounding vegetation and produces nodding, thick, leathery lavender to dull purple urn-shaped flowers with recurved petal tips in late spring and early summer, followed by the plumed seed heads typical of the leatherflower group. Because it is adapted to thin, rocky, calcium-rich soil in dappled shade at woodland edges, it is best grown on a modest fence or large shrub rather than a bare sunny trellis. Its very limited range makes it primarily a plant for conservation-minded native collections.

planting.note: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this low, non-climbing species belongs in a pine flatwoods or sandhill-style native bed rather than on a trellis.

directions: Pine hyacinth is a diminutive Florida endemic found in open pine flatwoods and sandhills, growing as a low, non-vining perennial with narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the climbing habit typical of most clematis. Its solitary, nodding, bell-shaped flowers range from lavender-pink to dusky maroon with distinctively recurved petal tips, and in its native range it can flower across much of the year whenever conditions allow. Adapted to deep sandy, fast-draining soil and frequent natural fire, it performs best in a lean, sunny native wildflower planting rather than a typical irrigated border. Its small size and unusual flower form make it a conversation piece for Florida native plant gardens.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, giving it a large fence, arbor, or shrub to climb into full sun.

directions: Golden clematis is the wild species behind the popular 'Bill MacKenzie' group of garden hybrids, native to rocky slopes and scrub from the western Himalaya through central Asia into China. It is a vigorous climber producing an abundance of nodding, bell-shaped, bright yellow flowers with thick, slightly waxy petals from midsummer into fall, followed by the large, silvery, fluffy seed heads shared by the whole tangutica group. Because it flowers on new growth, cut it back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter to keep it dense rather than bare at the base. It tolerates poor, lean soil and exposed sites better than most large-flowered clematis.

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, giving this vigorous climber a large pergola, wall, or mature tree to cover.

directions: This selection of the Himalayan anemone clematis produces an abundant late-spring flush of soft pink, single flowers with a light, sweet fragrance that carries well in the garden, covering the whole vine for several weeks before most other climbers have started. Like other montana-group clematis it is an extremely vigorous grower, best given a large wall, pergola, or old tree rather than a small trellis, since it can rapidly cover considerable vertical space. It flowers entirely on the previous year's wood, so prune immediately after flowering if size needs managing, never in winter or spring. Established plants need little care beyond an occasional thinning to prevent the tangled growth from becoming overly dense.

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, training onto a large support in full sun to light shade.

directions: This botanical variety of the Chinese anemone clematis flowers several weeks later than typical Clematis montana, extending the montana-group bloom season into early summer with white, star-shaped flowers set on distinctly longer stalks. The flowers carry a notably strong, sweet fragrance often compared to dark chocolate or ripe fruit, making it a favorite for planting near a seating area, doorway, or open window where the scent can be appreciated. As with other montana types it is a rampant grower suited only to large supports such as mature trees, high walls, or pergolas. Prune right after flowering, since next year's blooms form on the current season's wood.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown at soil level in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with roots kept cool by mulch or low companion plants.

directions: This pink-flowered selection of the non-vining solitary clematis keeps the same upright, herbaceous clumping habit as the species but trades the usual deep blue-violet for soft rose-pink, nodding, bell-shaped flowers with the same recurved, twisted petal tips from early to midsummer. Because it has no tendrils to climb with, let it sprawl loosely through neighboring perennials or stake it lightly at the front to middle of a mixed border. The flowers and the fluffy silver seed heads that follow both make good cut material. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches in late winter, since it flowers entirely on new growth each year.

planting.note: Plant against a sheltered, sunny wall or fence in well-drained soil; treat like the related evergreen winter clematis species, giving protection from the coldest winter winds.

directions: This evergreen selection comes from a Chinese species related to the more familiar Clematis armandii and cirrhosa and shares their glossy, leathery, drip-tipped foliage and winter-into-early-spring bloom season, opening nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers while most of the garden is dormant. It is a somewhat smaller, more restrained grower than armandii, making it easier to accommodate on a modest fence or wall in milder regions. Give it a sheltered, south- or west-facing spot out of harsh winter wind, since flower buds can be damaged by hard freezes. Prune lightly after flowering only to shape or control size, since it blooms on the previous season's growth.
